claims.text: Conventional stainless-steel passive films are insufficient under extreme corrosive conditions.
An ultrathin DFT-derived passivating film can be deposited on stainless steel using atomic layer deposition.
The proposed coating will significantly improve stainless-steel corrosion resistance relative to the untreated state.
Conventional stainless steel exhibits high corrosion rates in high-chloride or molten-salt environments.
The tailored coating introduces a more noble passivating surface layer.
The tailored coating introduces a densely packed passivating surface layer.
The passivating layer limits micro-galvanic activity.
The passivating layer limits aggressive electrochemical reactions.
DFT calculations can identify alloying elements and optimal surface compositions that increase the electrochemical stability of stainless-steel surfaces.
Increased surface electrochemical stability reduces localized corrosion initiated by environmental aggressors.
The coated steel will exhibit lower corrosion rates, including reduced weight loss, than untreated stainless steel under identical harsh conditions.
The coated steel will exhibit improved electrochemical profiles relative to untreated stainless steel.
Corrosion-resistance improvement depends on the coating being uniform, defect-free, and durable.
Mechanical damage or thermal cycling that compromises the film may reduce its corrosion-protection benefit.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement and the coating's long-term stability under cyclic or mechanical challenges are uncertain.
